claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by dynamic, strain-induced formation of a self-healing passive film.
Localized mechanical strain promotes surface segregation of oxidation-prone alloying elements.
The segregated oxidation-prone elements rapidly form and repair a protective oxide or hydroxide film.
The dynamically repaired passive film mitigates frictional wear.
The dynamically repaired passive film mitigates corrosive attack.
The proposed initial alloy is a homogeneous high-entropy alloy containing multiple principal elements and no preformed passive film.
Mechanical loading causes Cr, Al, or similar oxidation-prone elements to become enriched at the alloy surface.
Surface enrichment of oxidation-prone elements produces a stable, protective oxide or hydroxide film in situ.
Local deformation drives migration and enrichment of readily oxidized elements.
The resulting passive film is thin, adherent, and capable of repairing itself during ongoing wear.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the high-entropy alloy will have lower cumulative weight loss than a matched baseline lacking the proposed multi-element synergy.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the high-entropy alloy will sustain less surface damage than the matched baseline.
The protective effect occurs only when the wear rate leaves sufficient time for passive-film regeneration.
Excessive mechanical wear can remove the passive film faster than it reforms and thereby cause the protective mechanism to fail.
Sufficiently aggressive pH or ion concentrations can overwhelm the passive film and cause the protective mechanism to fail.
